output.title: Transcript Accuracy Is a Workflow Cost, Not a Feature
output.body:
If transcript accuracy matters to your business, the real question is not “is AI good enough?” It is: which recurring transcript task costs you more money and time today — manual checking, or accepting a draft that still needs review?

Treat accuracy as a bounded workflow decision. Separate the use case first: customer-facing meeting notes, internal call summaries, or text pulled from invoices and other records. Each one has a different tolerance for error. If the transcript feeds a high-risk decision, keep human approval in the loop. Money movement and other high-risk approvals should stay human anyway.

For a small business, the practical test is simple: pick one transcript task that repeats every week, then note two things for your own records — how long you spend verifying it, and what a single mistake would force you to fix. That gives you a real threshold instead of a vague feeling that “the transcript looked fine.” Fine is not a control.

If the task is low risk, a draft may be enough. If the task is customer-facing or affects approvals, accuracy needs a tighter review step. If it sits in medical, legal, or high-sensitivity financial work, Bareni treats that as current scope discipline, not a casual automation target.

That is usually the cleanest next step: choose one transcript workflow, measure the verification burden, and decide whether AI should stay a draft or become part of the process.
